title: EOS Auth and Security Analysis — Complete Current State and Target Architecture
revision_provenance: Revised in Phase 14.6F to align with 18 ratified P0 decisions (2026-06-04).
description: Complete auth and security analysis for EOS: current auth state across all code locations, target auth architecture, RLS implementation, session management, API security posture, data encryption, agent security model, privacy posture, identified vulnerabilities, migration path, and open questions requiring operator decision.
provenance_detail: Resolved from direct code inspection of transports/api/http/middleware/auth.ts (header-based org auth), transports/api/http/middleware/operator.ts (operator guard), transports/api/http/db/client.ts (dual-pool RLS architecture with withOrg()), transports/api/http/db/migrate.ts (14-table RLS policies, eos_app role creation), transports/api/http/db/schema.ts (users/orgs/members/approvals schema), transports/api/http/server.ts (route-level auth middleware binding), transports/api/http/package.json (dependency audit), substrate/types.py (PermissionTier 4-tier model, RiskClass, TIER_ACTION_MAP), substrate/control_plane/governance.py (deterministic governance engine), substrate/governance/policy/authority_engine.py (AuthorityEngine with risk classification and approval queuing), phase14_6b_eos_current_implementation_truth.json (Beast branch Clerk state, GitHub main Passport.js state), phase14_6b_eos_governance_permissions_model.json (RBAC+ABAC hybrid model).

details.session_store: Express session (likely memory or connect-pg-simple, unverified)
details.middleware: Single monolithic routes.ts with inline auth checks

problems: Passport.js is stateful session-based — incompatible with serverless/edge deployment
Firebase Auth adds a second identity provider alongside Passport — split-brain user identity
No middleware separation — auth logic inline with route handlers
No org/tenant scoping in auth layer
Replit Agent authored — no manual security review performed
Stale since Feb 2026 — 4 months of security patches not applied

details.clerk_react: ClerkProvider wrapping React app, SignIn/SignUp components
details.clerk_org: Clerk organizations for multi-tenant org switching
details.session_handling: Clerk manages sessions — JWTs, token refresh, device management all delegated
details.company_guard: CompanyGuard React component gates routes until org selected

beast_branch.assessment: Clerk integration is architecturally correct and represents the canonical codebase (ratified DEC-146B-EOS-001, DEC-146B-EOS-003, 2026-06-04). It replaces both Passport.js AND Firebase with a single identity provider. Middleware is properly separated. Org context flows through Clerk Organizations.

details.mechanism: Client sends x-org-id UUID header. Middleware validates UUID format, checks org exists in DB, sets orgId and userId (derived from org owner) on Hono context.
details.operator_guard: transports/api/http/middleware/operator.ts — verifies context user is org owner, re-validates against DB. Designed to work unchanged when real auth (signed sessions, bearer tokens) replaces the header mechanism.
details.identity_source: Org ownerId — NOT an independently authenticated user. This is the critical gap: any client that knows a valid org UUID can impersonate the owner.

umh_platform_layer.assessment: The UMH platform layer currently has NO real authentication. It has authorization (org-scoped, owner-verified) but identity is self-asserted via header. This is acceptable for solo-founder cockpit phase but is a P0 security gap before any multi-user or public deployment.

target_auth.decision_status: RESOLVED — Clerk ratified as production auth provider (DEC-146B-EOS-003, 2026-06-04, Phase 14.6C). Beast branch ratified as canonical codebase (DEC-146B-EOS-001, 2026-06-04, Phase 14.6C).
target_auth.rationale: Beast branch already has working Clerk integration. Clerk handles identity, sessions, MFA, OAuth, org management, device sessions. Eliminates need to build or maintain any of these. Single identity provider across SaaS frontend and UMH platform API.

magic_link.note: Clerk supports magic links natively. Decision needed: enable as primary passwordless flow or keep as fallback.

oauth_providers.rationale: Google confirmed via Beast Clerk config. Apple is standard for consumer-facing SaaS. Additional providers (GitHub, Microsoft) are trivial to enable in Clerk dashboard.

mfa.target: Clerk MFA — TOTP and SMS. Enforced for owner/admin tiers.

session_token_architecture.frontend: Clerk session token (JWT) — short-lived, auto-refreshed by Clerk SDK
session_token_architecture.api_calls: Bearer token in Authorization header — Clerk verifyToken() or clerkMiddleware()
session_token_architecture.umh_platform: Replace x-org-id header with Clerk JWT verification. Extract userId from Clerk token, orgId from Clerk Organization membership. Current operator_guard.ts needs zero changes — only auth.ts identity source changes.

integration_plan.step_1: Beast branch Clerk implementation is the canonical codebase (DEC-146B-EOS-001)
integration_plan.step_2: Add @clerk/backend to UMH platform API (transports/api/http/) — verify JWT, extract userId and orgId from Clerk session
integration_plan.step_3: Replace x-org-id header mechanism in auth.ts with Clerk token verification
integration_plan.step_4: Map Clerk Organization → EOS org_id in platform DB
integration_plan.step_5: Remove Passport.js and Firebase dependencies from merged codebase
integration_plan.step_6: Configure Clerk webhook to sync user/org creation to platform DB

current_state.mechanism: PostgreSQL RLS policies keyed to app.current_org_id GUC variable
current_state.enforcement: ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY + FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on all 14 tables

role_architecture.admin_role: neondb_owner — BYPASSRLS. Migrations and seeds only.
role_architecture.app_role: eos_app — No BYPASSRLS. RLS enforced. All application queries.

connection_pools.app_pool: DATABASE_APP_URL env var — eos_app credentials (falls back to DATABASE_URL if not set)

query_wrapper.mechanism: Opens transaction on app pool, SET LOCAL app.current_org_id, executes callback, commits/rollbacks. Transaction-scoped — never bleeds to other requests.
query_wrapper.fail_closed: Queries outside withOrg() on appDb return zero rows. By design.

gaps.description: DATABASE_APP_URL fallback to DATABASE_URL means if the env var is not set, all queries run as neondb_owner (BYPASSRLS). RLS is silently disabled.
gaps.remediation: Make DATABASE_APP_URL required (throw on missing), or at minimum log a warning when falling back to admin pool.

gaps.description: eos_app role creation in migrate.ts uses placeholder password: 'REPLACE_WITH_STRONG_PASSWORD'. If migration is run without changing this, the app role has a known weak credential.
gaps.remediation: Read password from environment variable EOS_APP_ROLE_PASSWORD. Fail migration if not set.

gaps.description: auth.ts uses admin db pool (not appDb) for org validation lookup. This is documented as intentional ('neondb_owner bypasses RLS, correct for auth checks') but means the auth middleware itself bypasses tenant isolation.
gaps.remediation: Acceptable for auth lookup (needs cross-tenant visibility). Document explicitly that admin pool is ONLY used in auth middleware and migration scripts.

gaps.description: users and portfolios tables are NOT in TENANT_TABLES list — they have no RLS policies. User emails and portfolio data are visible across tenants.
gaps.remediation: Add org_id to portfolios table (or scope via user_id → org membership join). Users table needs careful design — a user may belong to multiple orgs, so simple org_id RLS does not work. Consider a user_orgs join table with RLS.

rls.assessment: RLS implementation is architecturally sound — dual-pool model, transaction-scoped GUC, FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. The design is correct. The gaps are operational (env var fallback, placeholder password) and coverage (2 tables missing). P1 priority to close before any multi-tenant deployment.

umh_platform.mechanism: Stateless — no sessions. Each request sends x-org-id header. No session tokens, no cookies, no JWT.
umh_platform.user_agent_sessions_table: Exists in schema (user_agent_sessions) but tracks agent session state (which AI agent the user is talking to), NOT authentication sessions.

github_main.mechanism: Express session (connect-session, likely memory store or pg-simple). Passport.js serializes user to session. Firebase has its own session management.
problems: No session invalidation on password change

beast_branch.mechanism: Clerk-managed sessions. JWT-based. Short-lived access tokens with automatic refresh. Device session management. Multi-session support.

session_lifecycle.creation: Clerk handles on sign-in (OAuth, password, magic link, SSO)
session_lifecycle.storage: Clerk cloud — no session state in EOS database
session_lifecycle.invalidation: Clerk dashboard or API — immediate revocation across all devices
session_lifecycle.timeout: Configurable in Clerk dashboard (idle timeout + absolute timeout)

target.multi_device: Clerk supports concurrent sessions across devices. Session list visible to user.
target.impersonation: Clerk admin impersonation for support workflows. Logged and auditable.

rate_limiting.evidence: No rate limiting middleware in server.ts, no rate-limit package in package.json dependencies. Every endpoint is unbounded.
rate_limiting.target: Hono rate-limiter middleware or external (Cloudflare, Fly.io proxy). Per-org and per-IP limits.

cors.evidence: No CORS middleware in server.ts. No hono/cors import. Hono defaults to no CORS headers — browser cross-origin requests will fail, but server-to-server requests are unrestricted.
cors.target: Explicit CORS configuration — allowlist cockpit domain (universalmetaharness.tech), localhost for dev. Deny all others.

csrf.evidence: API is header-authenticated (x-org-id), not cookie-authenticated. CSRF attacks require cookie-based auth. When Clerk JWT is added via cookies (if using Clerk's cookie mode), CSRF protection becomes necessary.
csrf.target: If Clerk uses Authorization header (Bearer token) — CSRF is not applicable. If Clerk uses cookies — add Hono CSRF middleware or use SameSite=Strict.

input_validation.evidence: auth.ts validates UUID format for x-org-id. chat/converse validates content is non-empty string. No Zod validation middleware despite zod being in dependencies. Most routes cast req.json() to TypeScript types with 'as' — no runtime validation.
input_validation.target: Zod validation middleware on all POST/PUT/PATCH routes. Zod is already a dependency — wire it into a Hono middleware pattern.

error_handling.evidence: Global onError handler in server.ts catches unhandled errors, logs them, returns 500 with err.message. Risk: err.message may leak internal details (stack traces, DB errors, file paths) to the client.
error_handling.target: Sanitize error messages in production. Return generic 'Internal Server Error' to client, log full error server-side only.

request_size_limits.evidence: No explicit body size limit configured. Hono/node-server has default limits but they are generous. Large payloads could cause memory pressure.
request_size_limits.target: Explicit body size limit (e.g., 1MB for JSON, 10MB for file uploads).

security_headers.evidence: No helmet-equivalent middleware. No Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Strict-Transport-Security headers.
security_headers.target: Add Hono secureHeaders() middleware or equivalent. Critical for browser-facing endpoints.

at_rest.mechanism: Neon encrypts all data at rest by default (AES-256). No additional application-level encryption.
at_rest.assessment: Sufficient for current stage. Application-level field encryption (e.g., API keys, PII) is a future consideration for enterprise tier.

in_transit.database: TLS enforced by Neon (sslmode=require in connection strings). WebSocket connections also use TLS via @neondatabase/serverless.
in_transit.api: Depends on deployment. Fly.io provides TLS termination at edge. Local dev is plain HTTP.
in_transit.assessment: TLS coverage is adequate. No plaintext database connections possible (Neon enforces it).

sensitive_fields_unencrypted: API keys — managed by Clerk (not stored in EOS DB) but any integration API keys (if stored) would be plaintext
Agent conversation content — stored plaintext in interactions/messages
application_level.target: Field-level encryption for PII (emails, names) and integration credentials. pgcrypto extension is already enabled in migrations — can use pgp_sym_encrypt/decrypt.

agent_authority_bounds.description: UMH substrate enforces agent authority via a 4-tier permission model (READ < DRAFT < EXECUTE < COMMIT). Each EOS agent has a declared permission_tier that caps what actions it can perform.

agent_tiers.ceo: COMMIT — can execute payments, delete records, production deployments
agent_tiers.sales: EXECUTE — can send DMs, create outreach, book calls
agent_tiers.marketing: EXECUTE — can post content, send messages, publish
agent_tiers.finance: EXECUTE — can run bulk updates but NOT execute payments (that requires COMMIT)
agent_tiers.hr: DRAFT — can create tasks and documents, cannot execute externally
agent_tiers.legal: READ — analysis and research only, no mutations

risk_classification.enforcement: Deterministic-first. GovernanceEngine classifies by keyword/pattern matching before any AI involvement.
risk_classification.approval_flow: HIGH and CRITICAL actions are queued for operator approval via AuthorityEngine.queue_for_approval(). CRITICAL actions NEVER auto-execute regardless of autonomy level.

agent_authority_bounds.assessment: The authority model is well-designed and enforced at the substrate level. Every agent action passes through governance. The tier system prevents privilege escalation — an agent cannot perform actions above its declared tier.

details.browser_actions: Browser research and browser act are skills on every agent. Execution happens via adapters (browser adapter). No sandbox — the browser runs in the same process/container context.
details.container_execution: EXECUTE tier agents can spawn containers. Container isolation depends on Docker security (namespaces, cgroups) — not application-level sandboxing.
details.desktop_automation: Listed in EXECUTE tier actions. Would run on Beast node via Windows daemon. Sandboxing depends on Windows Service isolation.
details.code_execution: No direct code execution by agents in current implementation. Agent skills are Python functions, not arbitrary code execution.

gaps: No network isolation for agent browser sessions — agents could access internal services
No resource limits (CPU, memory, time) on individual agent task execution
No output size limits on agent responses
execution_sandboxing.target: Per-agent execution environments with resource limits, network policies, and output caps. UMH organism/workcell_protocol.py has workcell isolation patterns that can be extended.

current.mechanism: TIER_ACTION_MAP in substrate/types.py maps each permission tier to a frozen set of allowed action strings. required_tier_for_action() determines minimum tier for any action.
current.enforcement_point: GovernanceEngine._check_permission_tier() checks before execution. If caller tier is insufficient, action is blocked.
current.granularity: Action-type level (e.g., 'send_dm', 'execute_payment'). Not per-tool or per-resource.
current.audit: AuthorityEngine records approval requests and decisions. Governance decisions are logged.

gaps: No per-entity tool scoping — a sales agent with EXECUTE can send DMs for ANY entity in the org, not just assigned ones
No time-based access controls (e.g., no outreach outside business hours)
No budget/spend limits per agent per action type
No tool invocation audit trail separate from governance decisions

data_classification.what_exists: No formal data classification scheme. No fields marked as PII, sensitive, confidential, or public. Schema has no data_classification column or metadata.
data_classification.what_is_needed: Classify every field in schema as: PUBLIC, INTERNAL, CONFIDENTIAL, RESTRICTED. PII fields (email, name, conversation content) need CONFIDENTIAL or RESTRICTED classification. This classification drives encryption, retention, export, and deletion policies.

gaps: No right to erasure (Article 17) implementation — no user deletion flow
No data portability (Article 20) — no data export endpoint
No consent management — no record of what user consented to
No privacy policy or terms of service in application
No cookie consent (relevant when Clerk or PostHog uses cookies)
No Data Protection Officer designation (required if processing at scale)
gdpr.assessment: GDPR compliance is entirely unaddressed. For solo-founder phase this is acceptable. Before any EU user signs up, a compliance pass is mandatory.

ccpa.note: Similar gaps as GDPR. California Consumer Privacy Act applies if serving CA residents. Right to know, right to delete, right to opt-out of sale. No implementation.

data_retention.current: All data retained indefinitely. No TTL, no archival, no purge policy.
tables_needing_retention_policy: embeddings — vector data grows with every interaction
user_agent_sessions — session records never cleaned up
umh_outcomes — outcome log grows with every trace
data_retention.target: Define retention periods per data type. Implement automated archival/purge. Minimum: 90-day active, 1-year archive, then purge (except where legal hold applies).

data_residency.current: Neon Postgres region (likely us-east). No data residency controls.
data_residency.note: Enterprise customers may require data to stay in specific regions (EU, US, APAC). Neon supports regional databases. Not relevant until enterprise tier.

vulnerabilities.description: UMH platform API has no real authentication. Any client that knows a valid org UUID can impersonate the org owner by sending x-org-id header. The userId is derived from the org's ownerId, not from an authenticated session.
vulnerabilities.remediation: Replace x-org-id header mechanism with Clerk JWT verification. Extract userId from verified Clerk token. Map Clerk orgId to platform org via DB lookup or Clerk webhook sync.
vulnerabilities.timeline: Before any public or multi-user deployment. Acceptable for solo-founder cockpit phase.

vulnerabilities.description: DATABASE_APP_URL falls back to DATABASE_URL (admin/BYPASSRLS role) when not set. If deployment misconfigures env vars, all RLS policies are silently bypassed — every query sees all tenant data.
vulnerabilities.remediation: Remove fallback. Require DATABASE_APP_URL explicitly. Throw on startup if missing.

vulnerabilities.description: users and portfolios tables have no RLS policies. In multi-tenant deployment, any org can query any user's email/name and any portfolio data via the app pool.
vulnerabilities.affected_file: transports/api/http/db/migrate.ts (TENANT_TABLES array does not include users or portfolios)
vulnerabilities.remediation: Design cross-tenant user visibility model (users can belong to multiple orgs). Add portfolios to TENANT_TABLES with org_id scoping. For users, consider a membership-based RLS policy.

vulnerabilities.description: No rate limiting on any endpoint. An attacker (or misconfigured client) can exhaust server resources, flood the database, or abuse AI-powered endpoints (chat/converse) which trigger LLM calls.
vulnerabilities.remediation: Add rate limiting middleware. Critical endpoints (chat/converse, execution) need strict per-org limits. Health/system endpoints need IP-based limits.

vulnerabilities.description: Global error handler returns err.message to client. Database errors, file path leaks, and stack traces may be exposed in error responses.
vulnerabilities.remediation: In production, return generic error message to client. Log full error server-side. Use NODE_ENV check to control verbosity.

vulnerabilities.description: eos_app role migration uses hardcoded placeholder password 'REPLACE_WITH_STRONG_PASSWORD'. If migration runs without manual intervention, the DB role has a known weak password.
vulnerabilities.remediation: Read password from EOS_APP_ROLE_PASSWORD env var. Refuse to create role if env var is not set.

vulnerabilities.description: Most API routes accept JSON bodies cast to TypeScript types via 'as' without runtime validation. Malformed or malicious payloads pass through to business logic and database queries.
vulnerabilities.remediation: Add Zod validation middleware. Zod is already a dependency. Create a withValidation() helper that validates request body against schema before handler runs.

vulnerabilities.description: No security headers configured. Missing: Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Strict-Transport-Security, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy.
vulnerabilities.remediation: Add Hono secureHeaders() middleware from hono/secure-headers.

vulnerabilities.description: No automated dependency vulnerability scanning. package.json has 7 runtime dependencies — low surface area, but no CI/CD check for known CVEs.
vulnerabilities.remediation: Add npm audit to CI pipeline. Consider Dependabot or Renovate for automated security updates.

vulnerabilities.description: No per-entity scoping on agent actions. A sales agent with EXECUTE permission can send outreach for any entity in the org, not just the entity it is assigned to.
vulnerabilities.remediation: Add entity_scope to agent execution context. Governance engine checks entity assignment before permitting action.

passport_to_clerk.description: Beast feature/company-system branch (canonical codebase per DEC-146B-EOS-001) has fully replaced Passport.js + Firebase with Clerk (ratified per DEC-146B-EOS-003). React frontend uses ClerkProvider, SignIn/SignUp. Express backend uses clerkMiddleware(). Clerk Organizations for multi-tenant.
passport_to_clerk.remaining_work: Merge Beast branch to main. Remove all Passport.js and Firebase dependencies and dead code from merged result.

firebase_cleanup.description: GitHub main has Firebase Auth dependencies (firebase, firebase-admin). These must be removed during merge with canonical codebase. Firebase project can be decommissioned after merge.
files_to_remove: Firebase Auth imports in server routes

umh_platform_clerk_integration.description: transports/api/http/ needs @clerk/backend added to verify JWTs from the SaaS frontend. This replaces the x-org-id header mechanism. The operator_guard.ts is already designed to work without changes.
steps: Create Clerk client initialization (CLERK_SECRET_KEY env var)
Rewrite auth.ts to verify Bearer token via Clerk, extract userId and orgId
Add Clerk webhook handler to sync user/org creation to platform DB
Test: cockpit authenticates via Clerk, platform API validates JWT

open_questions.question: SSO provider selection: Clerk Enterprise SSO supports SAML and OIDC. Which identity providers should be supported at enterprise tier? (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace, custom SAML)
open_questions.impact: Determines Clerk plan tier and enterprise pricing

open_questions.question: Magic link authentication: Enable as primary passwordless flow, secondary fallback, or disabled?
open_questions.impact: Affects onboarding flow UX. Magic link reduces friction but some users prefer password.

open_questions.question: Enterprise auth features timeline: When do SSO, SCIM provisioning, and audit logs become requirements? Tied to which plan tier or customer size?
open_questions.impact: Determines when Clerk Enterprise plan is needed ($$$) and what infrastructure prep is needed now.

open_questions.question: Data residency requirements: Do we need to support EU-only, US-only, or other regional data storage for enterprise customers?
open_questions.impact: Affects database architecture (multi-region Neon), Clerk configuration, and compliance posture.

open_questions.question: MFA enforcement policy: Require MFA for all users, only owner/admin, or make it optional with org-level policy?
open_questions.impact: Security vs. friction tradeoff. Recommendation: require for owner/admin, optional for member/viewer.

open_questions.question: Agent execution audit retention: How long should agent action logs, governance decisions, and approval records be retained?
open_questions.impact: Compliance, storage costs, and forensic capability. Financial actions may have legal retention requirements.

open_questions.question: API key authentication: Should EOS support API key auth for programmatic access (integrations, CI/CD, third-party apps) in addition to Clerk sessions?
open_questions.impact: Determines if we need a separate API key table, rotation mechanism, and scope-limited permissions.

security_posture_summary.rationale: The system has strong architectural foundations (RLS, permission tiers, governance engine, dual-pool DB) but lacks the authentication layer that ties it all together. The x-org-id header mechanism means all authorization infrastructure is built on an unauthenticated identity assertion. Once Clerk JWT verification replaces the header, the security posture jumps to PRODUCTION_READY_SINGLE_TENANT. Multi-tenant production requires closing the RLS gaps and adding rate limiting.
strengths: RLS architecture is correct: dual-pool, transaction-scoped, FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on 14 tables
Permission tier model is well-designed: 4 tiers, cumulative, with explicit action mappings
Governance engine is deterministic-first: no AI dependency for security decisions
Authority engine queues HIGH/CRITICAL actions for operator approval
CRITICAL actions never auto-execute regardless of autonomy level
Operator guard is pre-designed for real auth integration (zero changes needed)
Fail-closed design: queries outside withOrg() return zero rows
critical_gaps: No real authentication — identity is self-asserted via header
No rate limiting on any endpoint
RLS fallback silently disables tenant isolation
2 tables (users, portfolios) have no RLS policies
No input validation middleware despite Zod being available
priority_order: P0: Replace x-org-id with Clerk JWT verification (VULN-001)
P0: Make DATABASE_APP_URL required, remove fallback (VULN-002)
P1: Add users/portfolios to RLS coverage (VULN-003)
P1: Sanitize error responses in production (VULN-005)
